\section{Introduction}

A companion study measured whether one state's official legal record was
available and internally consistent when someone tried to build on it, and
found that neither could be assumed.\footnote{Cited as a companion study so
this article can be read on its own; the corpus and analysis are openly
published.} It ended with a proposal --- a five-field provenance schema that a
publisher of official data could populate at the point of collection --- and
with a weakness it stated plainly: one jurisdiction, and an argument rather than
a demonstration that the method travels.

This article is the demonstration, and it is not a replication. Repeating a
measurement in a second place tests whether a number recurs. Applying an
instrument in a second place tests the instrument. The second is the more useful
thing to do with a proposal, and it is what this article reports: what the
schema captured, what it missed, and what had to change in it.

The jurisdiction was chosen so that the answer would be informative whichever
way it came out. The United Kingdom's official legislation service is, by any
ordinary standard, well run. It publishes a documented interface, permanent
identifiers for every provision, and machine-readable metadata alongside every
text. If the companion study's findings were about a particular state's
capacity, almost nothing here should be measurable.

Something is, and it is not what the companion study looked for. The service
publishes, in each Act's own metadata, a list of amendments that have been
enacted and that it has \emph{not} incorporated into the text it displays. It
declares this rather than concealing it. It states a target for clearing them.
And a reader still cannot tell, for any particular provision, whether the
declared defect is a week old or a decade old --- because the field that would
answer that is not published.

That is the shape of the finding, and it is the opposite of the companion
study's. There, the defect had to be excavated: four instruments whose portal
text disagreed with the portal's own amendment log, each found by hand. Here it
is handed to the reader, at scale, per provision, in a form a machine can read
--- and it is still not enough. The gap between those two cases is what this
article is about.

\section{What the service publishes about its own currency}

Two features of \texttt{legislation.gov.uk} matter here, and both are the
publisher's own statements rather than this study's inferences.

The first is the \emph{unapplied effect}. When an amendment has been made to an
Act and the revised text has not yet been changed to reflect it, the service
records the fact in the Act's metadata and flags it to readers: `If the primary
legislation on legislation.gov.uk has any unapplied effects, we flag them in
the ``Changes to Legislation'' banner on the website. Clicking on the banner
reveals the outstanding changes.'\footnote{\emph{Understanding legislation},
\url{https://www.legislation.gov.uk/understanding-legislation}, under the
heading `Our editorial practice and timescales'. The heading matters: the same
page carries a separate section on legislation originating from the EU, and
the commitment quoted here sits outside it and is stated generally.}
Each such effect names the amending instrument, the provision affected, and the
kind of change.

The second is a service standard: `We aim to incorporate new amendments into
the text of the legislation within three months of those amendments coming into
force.'\footnote{Ibid., same heading.}

The standard matters as much for what it rules out as for what it establishes.
A three-month target means the expected steady state is not zero unapplied
effects; a queue is the design, not the defect. Any finding here has to be
about the queue's tail rather than its existence, and the analysis is built
accordingly.

\section{Method}

\paragraph{Collection.} Every Public General Act from \nYearFrom{} to
\nYearTo{} was enumerated from the service's own year feeds, and each Act's
metadata retrieved from its \texttt{introduction/data.xml} endpoint. That
endpoint carries the complete unapplied-effects block --- verified rather than
assumed, by comparing it against the full text and the contents listing for the
same Act and finding the same effects in all three --- at a fraction of the
bytes. The service's
\texttt{robots.txt} declares a five-second crawl delay and the collector
honours it, which is why a sweep of the statute book takes hours.

\paragraph{The schema, populated at collection time.} The companion study's
five fields were written for each record as it was retrieved, unchanged from
that paper's definition. This is the point of the exercise rather than
decoration: that paper claims the schema costs nothing because a collector that
knows how it obtained a document already knows all five values. Populating them
prospectively is the only way to find out whether that is true.

\paragraph{What is measured, and what is not.} The companion study measured two
properties: availability and internal consistency. Only the second is compared
here, and the reason is structural rather than practical. Four of the schema's
five fields describe the \emph{encounter} --- whether the live source answered
this collector, on this network, on this day --- and encounters do not compare
across collections, because they differ before the records do. No control
corrects for that. Availability figures are recorded and published for this
collection, and are not set against the companion study's.

An unapplied effect has no such problem. It is a property of the data as
published: any reader, on any network, at any time, obtains the same count.

\section{What the schema learned about itself}

Two changes to the companion study's proposal came out of using it, and neither
would have come out of thinking about it.

\paragraph{A discrepancy has to record who declared it.} Applied to a well-run
interface, four of the five fields take a single value across every record in
the collection: one source class, one retrieval route, one corroboration count,
one transformation. That is the schema working, not failing --- it costs
nothing here because there is nothing to say.

But the defect this study measures was invisible to all five fields. An Act
whose displayed text omits hundreds of enacted amendments was retrieved
perfectly: official primary source, live, no transformation, nothing to report.
Under the schema as written, it is indistinguishable from an Act with no
unapplied effects at all.

The remedy is not a sixth field. The purpose the companion study gives
\texttt{discrepancy} is `is there a known problem with this record?', and a
publisher flagging its own text as not current is exactly that. What the
field's \emph{values} omit is that a discrepancy can be declared by the source
as well as found by the collector --- and a null means different things in the
two cases. Found by a collector, it cost two or more sources and a comparison,
so a null may only mean nobody looked hard enough. Declared by a source, it
costs nothing to record, so a null means the publisher did not say. A single
null standing for both is the collapse that paper objects to when one
confidence score stands for availability and consistency at once.

The two jurisdictions are the argument. Here, \nDiscrepancyDeclared{} records
carry a source-declared discrepancy and \nDiscrepancyFound{} a collector-found
one. In the companion corpus it was the reverse: four self-contradicting
instruments, every one of them found by hand. The same class of defect, with
opposite provenance --- and a straightforward consequence for who should be
doing the work.

\paragraph{The fields divide by what they describe, not by what they are
about.} \texttt{source\_class} describes the record: whose copy this is.
\texttt{retrieval\_route}, \texttt{corroboration} and \texttt{transformation}
describe the encounter: whether the live source answered \emph{us}, how many
sources \emph{we} found agreeing, what \emph{we} had to do to the bytes we got.
\texttt{discrepancy} is either, depending on who declared it.

Four of five describe the encounter, which is why the availability half of this
comparison could not be salvaged. It also complicates the companion study's own
recommendation. That paper asks publishers to populate these fields; if a
publisher does, the encounter fields describe the publisher's encounter with
its own source, which is a third thing again and comparable with neither. A
provenance schema intended for use across collections has to mark which of its
fields are encounter-relative. That one does not.

\section{Limits}

\paragraph{The age of an amendment is not published.} Every age reported here
is the age of the \emph{amending instrument}, which is the only date the
service exposes. It is not the date the amendment came into force, and the two
can be decades apart: \nBackwardEffects{} effects in this collection have an
affecting instrument older than the Act it amends, because provisions that were
never commenced bite, when commenced, on a later consolidating Act. Compliance
with the three-month target therefore cannot be computed from what the service
publishes --- which is itself among the findings, but it also bounds every age
figure here.

\paragraph{Denominators are choices, and all of them are reported.} An Act the
service serves as enacted rather than in revised form has no revised text for
an amendment to be missing from; a wholly repealed Act has no live text at all.
Excluding them raises the affected share and including them lowers it. Neither
is obviously right, so the article reports the share on all three bases rather
than choosing one.

\paragraph{Coverage.} \nActsListed{} Acts were listed and \nActsRetrieved{}
retrieved. Retrieval failures were recorded rather than retried away while
availability was in scope; once it left the comparison, a second pass recovered
what it could, and both attempts are kept in the record.

\paragraph{The modern statute book, and a lower bound.} The sweep covers
Public General Acts from \nYearFrom{} to \nYearTo{}. That range was chosen on
the assumption that unapplied effects accumulate in modern legislation, and the
assumption is wrong: a sample of twenty Acts drawn from before it found five
carrying unapplied effects and \nPreSampleEffects{} effects in total, the
Highways Act 1980 alone accounting for \nHighwaysEffects{}. Every total
reported here is therefore a lower bound on the statute book as a whole rather
than a census of it, and the concentration figures are computed within the
period covered.

Extending the sweep is a matter of time rather than method --- at the
publisher's declared crawl delay the pre-1988 book is many hours of collection
--- and the range is stated rather than quietly presented as complete.

\paragraph{Primary legislation only.} Statutory instruments are not covered.
They are the larger population and carry their own unapplied effects; nothing
here should be read as a statement about them.

\paragraph{A note on the subject.} This article measures a defect that
\texttt{legislation.gov.uk} discloses about itself. It is not an accusation.
Almost no comparable publisher discloses as much, which is what makes the
measurement possible at all, and the article's argument is that disclosure of
this quality still leaves a reader unable to answer the question it raises.
